C005.subject: bottlenecks in current machine learning architectures
C005.object: memory bandwidth limitations in distributed training
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: bottlenecks in current machine learning architectures memory bandwidth limitations in distributed training]

[PATH:empirical] Systematic profiling of large-scale training runs (e.g., using PyTorch Profiler or TensorBoard) on models like GPT-3 or LLaMA-65B to measure the fraction of time spent on memory-bound operations (e.g., all-reduce, data loading) vs. compute-bound operations. — Direct measurement of memory bandwidth utilization in distributed training of >1B parameter models can confirm whether it is the primary bottleneck, or if other factors (e.g., communication latency, kernel overhead) dominate.

[PATH:theoretical] Roofline model analysis applied to transformer-based architectures on distributed GPU clusters (e.g., using NVIDIA Nsight Compute), comparing arithmetic intensity of forward/backward passes to the memory bandwidth ceiling of the hardware. — A roofline model provides a formal framework to determine if performance is bound by memory bandwidth or compute. This can refute the hypothesis if the bottleneck is instead compute-bound (e.g., due to inefficient attention mechanisms).

[PATH:literature] Literature review of recent papers on distributed training efficiency (e.g., from MLSys, NeurIPS, or SC conferences) that isolate memory bandwidth as a key variable, such as studies on gradient compression, pipeline parallelism, or memory-efficient attention. — Synthesizing findings from multiple studies can reveal whether the community consensus attributes scaling bottlenecks to memory bandwidth or to other factors like network topology or synchronisation overhead, thus confirming or refuting the hypothesis.

scope.domain: deep learning systems with >1 billion parameters

[PATH:literature] Systematic literature review of recent (2023-2024) papers on data curation, deduplication, and augmentation strategies for large-scale deep learning systems, focusing on reported performance gains. — Aggregates evidence from multiple studies to assess consensus on whether data improvements consistently yield larger gains than architectural innovations.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical analysis of information-theoretic capacity bounds in overparameterized models, examining how data diversity affects the effective dimensionality of learned representations. — Provides a formal framework to determine if insufficient data diversity is a fundamental limitation distinct from model capacity or optimization constraints.

C007.subject: bottlenecks in current machine learning architectures
C007.object: the lack of a closed-loop sensorimotor feedback mechanism that enforces causal consistency across long-horizon tasks
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: bottlenecks in current machine learning architectures the lack of a closed-loop sensorimotor feedback mechanism that enforces causal consistency across long-horizon tasks]

[PATH:empirical] Comparative ablation studies on state-of-the-art model-based RL agents (e.g., DreamerV3, TD-MPC2) with and without explicit causal consistency constraints in their latent dynamics over long horizons. — Directly tests whether adding a closed-loop causal consistency mechanism improves long-horizon task performance, confirming or refuting the hypothesis that its absence is a primary bottleneck.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical analysis of sample complexity bounds for partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) with sensorimotor feedback vs. open-loop policies. — Provides formal characterization of how closed-loop feedback affects learning efficiency and causal identifiability, offering a principled foundation to evaluate the hypothesis.

[PATH:literature] Survey and meta-analysis of recent (2020–2025) failures in long-horizon robotic manipulation tasks, focusing on whether breakdowns correlate with lack of sensorimotor feedback or with other factors (e.g., reward sparsity, model capacity). — Contextualizes the hypothesis within established empirical findings, identifying whether the proposed causal mechanism is a common missing ingredient across reported bottlenecks.

C008.subject: bottlenecks in current machine learning architectures
C008.object: limitations in computational resources and algorithmic inefficiencies
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: bottlenecks in current machine learning architectures limitations in computational resources and algorithmic inefficiencies]

[PATH:empirical] Comparative analysis of sample efficiency and wall-clock time in deep reinforcement learning algorithms (e.g., SAC, PPO, Dreamer) on standard robotic control benchmarks (DM Control, MuJoCo) under fixed computational budgets — Directly tests whether performance plateaus are due to computational resource limits (e.g., GPU memory, simulation speed) versus algorithmic inefficiencies (e.g., sample complexity, credit assignment). Comparing scaling curves (e.g., returns vs. compute) across algorithms can isolate the primary bottleneck.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical analysis of the computational complexity of policy gradient methods and model-based RL, focusing on reliance on large batch sizes, replay buffers, and iterative dynamics models — Provides formal bounds on how algorithmic choices (e.g., on-policy vs. off-policy, model accuracy vs. planning depth) interact with hardware constraints. If theoretical lower bounds exceed practical compute, it confirms the hypothesis; if not, it suggests other bottlenecks (e.g., exploration, reward sparsity).

[PATH:literature] Recent literature reviews on scaling laws in robotics and RL (e.g., 'Scaling Data and Compute in Robotics' from 2022-2024 workshops, or studies on the 'bitter lesson' applied to RL) — Synthesizes empirical findings across many studies to identify whether compute scaling consistently yields diminishing returns in robotics RL versus other domains (e.g., NLP), and whether algorithmic innovations (e.g., Hindsight Experience Replay, curiosity-driven exploration) overcome resource limits or introduce new inefficiencies.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of recent literature on bottlenecks in embodied AI (e.g., review papers on sim-to-real transfer, generalization in multi-modal models) — Synthesizes existing empirical findings across multiple studies to assess whether reported bottlenecks consistently correlate with architectural complexity or with insufficient grounded training, thereby evaluating the hypothesis at a broader scope.

C010.subject: bottlenecks in current machine learning architectures
C010.object: insufficient architectural complexity and lack of advanced training techniques
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: bottlenecks in current machine learning architectures insufficient architectural complexity and lack of advanced training techniques]

[PATH:empirical] Comparative scaling-law analysis of transformer architectures with and without advanced training techniques (e.g., mixture-of-experts, curriculum learning) on multi-modal benchmarks like Meta-World or Habitat — Directly tests whether increasing architectural complexity (e.g., deeper networks, sparse attention) and advanced training methods (e.g., adaptive optimizers, reinforcement learning from human feedback) alleviate known bottlenecks in sample efficiency and generalization for embodied AI.

[PATH:literature] Survey of recent literature on bottlenecks in multi-modal foundation models (e.g., PaLM-E, Gato, RT-2) focusing on identified failure modes: data integration, long-horizon planning, and sim-to-real transfer — Provides a systematic review of whether current bottlenecks are attributed to insufficient complexity or other factors (e.g., data quality, compute limits), helping to refute or support the hypothesis by synthesizing expert consensus.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical analysis of representational capacity in constrained architectures (e.g., limited-depth transformers vs. universal approximators) applied to multi-modal reasoning tasks — Evaluates whether known theoretical bounds on expressivity and learnability imply that increased complexity is necessary for overcoming bottlenecks, or if training techniques alone could suffice.
